narrative: Your application for university admission was unfortunately rejected because our predictive model indicates a 99.2% probability that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. This assessment is based on several factors, most notably your academic standing during law school, where your first and third-year grades placed you in the bottom 20% of your class. Compared to students who typically pass the exam, who usually rank in the top 60%, your current academic trajectory presents a significant challenge. To help you understand this decision, we looked at "what if" scenarios—alternative versions of your profile that would have resulted in an admission approval. These scenarios identify the smallest possible changes needed to shift the model’s prediction from a failure to a passing result. By analyzing these three different scenarios, we can pinpoint exactly which parts of your application were the most influential in the model's final determination. Across all three scenarios generated, the model consistently focused on a single factor: your undergraduate grade point average. While your LSAT score of 34 is slightly below the average of 37 for passing students, and your family's upper-middle-income status is generally a positive indicator, the model found your undergraduate GPA of 2.9 to be the most critical pivot point. Interestingly, in every single alternative scenario, a minor adjustment to this GPA was the only change required to flip the prediction to a "pass." This indicates that your undergraduate performance, when combined with your law school decile rankings, is the primary reason for the current rejection. Because your law school rankings in both your first and third years are currently at a 2.0 decile, the model is extremely sensitive to how your earlier undergraduate work balances out your more recent performance. To improve your chances for a future application, focusing on demonstrating a higher level of academic mastery in a legal context is essential. While you cannot change your past undergraduate GPA, the model's reliance on this feature suggests that your current law school grades are not yet high enough to overcome that specific historical data point. If you were to raise your law school performance closer to the average decile of 6.0 seen in successful candidates, the influence of your undergraduate GPA would likely diminish. Strengthening your LSAT score toward the average of 37.27 would also provide a more robust cushion against the model's concerns regarding your academic history. Ultimately, the path to an approved application involves narrowing the gap between your current rankings and the typical performance levels of students who successfully clear the bar. By focusing on these specific academic metrics, you can shift the probability in your favor for future admissions cycles.
